questions.question: What are atomic classes and CAS?
questions.answer: AtomicInteger etc. use Compare-And-Swap hardware instructions for lock-free thread-safe updates.

questions.question: CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier vs Semaphore?
questions.answer: Latch: one-time wait for N events. Barrier: reusable, threads wait for each other. Semaphore: limits concurrent access via permits.

questions.question: What is ThreadLocal and what is its risk?
questions.answer: Per-thread variable copy. In thread pools it can leak memory or stale data if not removed with remove().

questions.question: What are virtual threads (Project Loom)?
questions.answer: Lightweight JVM-managed threads (Java 21) that make blocking IO cheap, enabling thread-per-request at high scale.

questions.question: What is a race condition? Give an example.
questions.answer: Outcome depends on thread timing. Example: two threads doing count++ (read-modify-write) can lose updates.

questions.question: What is the Fork/Join framework?
questions.answer: Divide-and-conquer parallelism with work-stealing. Parallel streams use the common ForkJoinPool.

questions.question: Explain JVM memory areas.
questions.answer: Heap (objects), Metaspace (class metadata), thread stacks (frames), PC registers, native method stacks.

questions.question: How does garbage collection work?
questions.answer: GC finds unreachable objects from GC roots and reclaims them. Generational: young (eden, survivors) collected often, old collected rarely.

questions.question: G1 vs ZGC vs Parallel GC?
questions.answer: Parallel: max throughput. G1: balanced default with pause targets. ZGC: ultra-low pauses (sub-millisecond) for large heaps.

questions.question: What causes OutOfMemoryError and how do you debug it?
questions.answer: Heap leak, too many classes (Metaspace), too many threads. Take a heap dump (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError) and analyze with MAT or VisualVM.

questions.question: StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError?
questions.answer: StackOverflowError: deep or infinite recursion exhausting thread stack. OutOfMemoryError: heap or native memory exhausted.

questions.question: What are strong, soft, weak and phantom references?
questions.answer: Strong: never collected while reachable. Soft: collected under memory pressure (caches). Weak: collected at next GC (WeakHashMap). Phantom: post-finalization cleanup hooks.

questions.question: How does class loading work?
questions.answer: Bootstrap, Platform and Application class loaders with parent delegation. Steps: loading, linking (verify, prepare, resolve), initialization.

questions.question: What is a memory leak in Java and common causes?
questions.answer: Objects still referenced but unused: static collections, unclosed resources, listeners not removed, ThreadLocals, bad caches.

questions.question: What is the JIT compiler?
questions.answer: Compiles hot bytecode to native code at runtime with optimizations like inlining and escape analysis (C1 and C2 tiers).

questions.question: What are lambda expressions and functional interfaces?
questions.answer: Lambdas are concise anonymous functions. A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (Runnable, Function, Predicate).

questions.question: map() vs flatMap() in streams?
questions.answer: map transforms one-to-one. flatMap transforms each element to a stream and flattens the result.

questions.question: Intermediate vs terminal stream operations?
questions.answer: Intermediate (filter, map) are lazy and return a stream. Terminal (collect, forEach, reduce) trigger processing.

questions.question: What is Optional and how should it be used?
questions.answer: A container for a possibly absent value. Use as a return type only; avoid in fields and parameters; prefer orElseGet, map, ifPresent over get().

questions.question: When should you avoid parallel streams?
questions.answer: Small datasets, blocking IO, stateful or ordered operations, or shared mutable state. The common pool is shared across the JVM.

questions.question: What are default and static methods in interfaces?
questions.answer: Allow adding behavior to interfaces without breaking implementers; also resolve the diamond problem by explicit override with Interface.super.method().

questions.question: Collectors.groupingBy example?
questions.answer: list.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Employee::getDept, Collectors.counting())) returns a Map of department to count.

questions.question: What is Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection?
questions.answer: The container creates and wires objects instead of your code. DI types: constructor (preferred), setter, field.

questions.question: Spring bean scopes?
questions.answer: singleton (default), prototype, request, session, application, websocket.

questions.question: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository vs @Controller?
questions.answer: All are stereotype annotations for component scanning. @Repository adds exception translation; @Controller handles web requests; @Service marks business logic.

questions.question: @Autowired vs constructor injection?
questions.answer: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and final, eases testing, and prevents partially constructed objects.

questions.question: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?
questions.answer: @EnableAutoConfiguration loads conditional configuration classes (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean) from the classpath and properties.

questions.question: How does @Transactional work and what are its pitfalls?
questions.answer: Implemented with AOP proxies. Self-invocation bypasses the proxy, private methods are ignored, and by default only unchecked exceptions trigger rollback.

questions.question: Transaction propagation types?
questions.answer: REQUIRED (default), REQUIRES_NEW, NESTED, SUPPORTS, NOT_SUPPORTED, MANDATORY, NEVER.

questions.question: What is a circular dependency and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: Beans depending on each other. Fix by redesign, setter injection, or @Lazy; constructor-based cycles fail at startup.

questions.question: How do you handle exceptions globally in Spring MVC?
questions.answer: Use @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods to return consistent error responses.

questions.question: What is Spring AOP?
questions.answer: Aspect-oriented programming for cross-cutting concerns (logging, transactions, security) using proxies, with advice types Before, After, Around.

questions.question: How do you secure a REST API in Spring?
questions.answer: Spring Security filter chain with JWT or OAuth2, method-level @PreAuthorize, stateless sessions, CORS and CSRF configured appropriately.

questions.question: What is the bean lifecycle?
questions.answer: Instantiate, populate dependencies, Aware callbacks, BeanPostProcessor, @PostConstruct, ready for use, @PreDestroy on shutdown.

questions.question: What is the N+1 problem and how do you solve it?
questions.answer: One query for parents plus N queries for lazy children. Fix with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, or batch fetching.

questions.question: Lazy vs eager loading?
questions.answer: Lazy loads associations on first access (can cause LazyInitializationException outside a session). Eager loads immediately, often over-fetching.

questions.question: First-level vs second-level cache?
questions.answer: First-level is per Session/EntityManager and on by default. Second-level is shared across sessions and must be configured (Ehcache, Redis).

questions.question: Entity states in JPA?
questions.answer: Transient (new), Managed (persistent), Detached, Removed.

questions.question: get() vs load() in Hibernate?
questions.answer: get() hits the DB immediately and returns null if missing. load() returns a proxy and throws an exception on access if missing.

questions.question: How do you handle optimistic vs pessimistic locking?
questions.answer: Optimistic uses a @Version column and fails on conflict. Pessimistic locks rows (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE).

questions.question: What are ACID properties and isolation levels?
questions.answer: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability. Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable.

questions.question: How do database indexes help and what is their cost?
questions.answer: They speed up reads (usually B-tree), but slow writes and use storage. Index selective columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY.

questions.question: Monolith vs microservices trade-offs?
questions.answer: Microservices give independent deployment and scaling but add network latency, distributed data and operational complexity.

questions.question: What is the Circuit Breaker pattern?
questions.answer: Stops calls to a failing service after a threshold, fails fast, then half-opens to test recovery (Resilience4j).

questions.question: How do you handle distributed transactions?
questions.answer: Saga pattern (choreography or orchestration) with compensating actions, plus idempotent operations; avoid 2PC where possible.

questions.question: What is idempotency and why does it matter for APIs?
questions.answer: Repeating a request has the same effect as once. Essential for safe retries; use idempotency keys for POST.

questions.question: REST best practices?
questions.answer: Resource-based URLs, correct HTTP verbs and status codes, statelessness, versioning, pagination, consistent error format.

questions.question: How do you make an API scalable and fast?
questions.answer: Caching (Redis), DB indexing, pagination, async processing with queues (Kafka/RabbitMQ), horizontal scaling, connection pooling.

questions.question: Kafka vs RabbitMQ?
questions.answer: Kafka: distributed log, high throughput, replayable events, partitioned consumers. RabbitMQ: traditional broker with flexible routing and per-message acknowledgment.

questions.question: Explain the CAP theorem.
questions.answer: During a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability.

questions.question: Common design patterns used in real projects?
questions.answer: Factory, Builder, Singleton, Strategy, Observer, Decorator, Proxy, Adapter, Template Method.

questions.question: Production API suddenly became slow. How do you troubleshoot?
questions.answer: Check metrics and logs, take thread dumps (blocked threads), check GC logs and heap, inspect slow DB queries and connection pool, trace downstream calls, review recent deployments.

questions.question: CPU is at 100% on a Java service. What do you do?
questions.answer: Find the hot thread with top -H, convert its id to hex, match it in a jstack dump; also check for GC thrash or infinite loops.

questions.question: How would you design a rate limiter?
questions.answer: Token bucket or sliding window, stored in Redis with atomic operations, keyed by user or IP, returning HTTP 429.

questions.question: How do you find duplicates in a list efficiently?
questions.answer: Use a HashSet while iterating (O(n)), or stream groupingBy with counting.

questions.question: How do you ensure thread safety in a shared cache?
questions.answer: Use ConcurrentHashMap with computeIfAbsent, or Caffeine/Guava cache with eviction; avoid check-then-act races.

questions.question: How do you handle large file processing without OOM?
questions.answer: Stream with BufferedReader or Files.lines, process in chunks or batches, avoid loading the entire file into memory.

questions.question: How do you test your code?
questions.answer: JUnit 5 and Mockito for unit tests, @SpringBootTest and Testcontainers for integration tests, test pyramid, meaningful coverage over raw percentage.

questions.question: How do you implement logging and monitoring?
questions.answer: SLF4J with Logback, structured logs with correlation IDs, metrics via Micrometer and Prometheus/Grafana, tracing with OpenTelemetry.

questions.question: Explain a challenging bug you solved or a design decision you made.
questions.answer: Use STAR format: Situation, Task, Action, Result. Highlight root-cause analysis, trade-offs and measurable impact.

questions.question: Coding task: reverse a linked list, detect a cycle, and find the first non-repeating character.
questions.answer: Reverse: iterate with prev, curr, next pointers. Cycle: Floyd slow/fast pointers. First non-repeating char: LinkedHashMap of counts, then return first with count 1.

data.title: Java Backend Developer Interview Preparation: Project Deep Dives and System Design
data.target_experience: Approximately 1–3 years; includes fundamentals that interviewers may probe more deeply
data.important_note: The project answers below are model answers and example designs, not claims about the candidate's actual work. Replace technologies, decisions, responsibilities and metrics with details that are true for your own project. Never invent production traffic, impact or ownership.

debugging: Write a root-cause and prevention plan

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: Explain your project in 60–90 seconds.
questions.answer: Start with the user problem, then the main features, architecture, your personal contribution, one challenge and the outcome. Example: “This service exposes REST APIs, validates requests, applies business rules in a service layer, persists data through Spring Data JPA, and returns consistent responses.”
questions.short_explanation: Give the interviewer a clear map before diving into details.
questions.likely_follow_up: What was your individual contribution? What would you improve?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: Why did you choose this technology stack?
questions.answer: Tie each technology to a requirement: Java for maintainable backend logic, Spring Boot for application setup and REST support, relational storage for transactional data, and automated tests for regression protection.
questions.short_explanation: Avoid saying you chose a tool only because it is popular.
questions.likely_follow_up: What alternative did you consider?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: Draw your project architecture and explain one request end to end.
questions.answer: A typical layered flow is client → controller → validation → service/business rules → repository → database, then the response flows back through DTO mapping and exception handling.
questions.short_explanation: Be able to explain where each responsibility lives and why.
questions.likely_follow_up: Where is authorization checked? Where are transactions applied?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: Why separate controller, service and repository layers?
questions.answer: Controllers handle HTTP concerns, services implement use cases and transaction boundaries, and repositories handle persistence access.
questions.short_explanation: Layering reduces coupling and makes business logic easier to test.
questions.likely_follow_up: What logic should not be placed in a controller?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: Why use DTOs instead of returning JPA entities directly?
questions.answer: DTOs define the external API contract and prevent accidental exposure of internal fields; they also help control validation and response shape.
questions.short_explanation: Entity changes should not automatically become public API changes.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you map between entity and DTO?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: How do you validate incoming requests?
questions.answer: Use Bean Validation annotations at the API boundary, invoke validation with @Valid, and perform business validation in the service layer.
questions.short_explanation: Syntactic validation and business-rule validation solve different problems.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you return field-level validation errors?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: How do you handle exceptions consistently?
questions.answer: Use @RestControllerAdvice and @ExceptionHandler to map known failures to stable error bodies and suitable HTTP status codes; log unexpected errors with a correlation ID.
questions.short_explanation: Do not return stack traces or internal details to clients.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you distinguish 400, 404 and 409?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: How do you manage database transactions?
questions.answer: Place @Transactional around a use case that must succeed or fail atomically, keep the transaction focused, and understand rollback rules and proxy behavior.
questions.short_explanation: A transaction should protect a business invariant, not simply wrap every method.
questions.likely_follow_up: What happens if an exception is thrown midway?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: How do you avoid exposing sensitive information?
questions.answer: Apply authentication and authorization, validate inputs, return only allowed DTO fields, keep secrets outside source control, and avoid logging tokens or personal data.
questions.short_explanation: Security must be applied at both endpoint and business-object level.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you prevent a user accessing another user's record?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: How did you test your project?
questions.answer: Use unit tests for business rules, MVC/controller tests for HTTP behavior, repository tests for persistence queries, and integration tests for critical end-to-end paths.
questions.short_explanation: Test both expected results and important failure cases.
questions.likely_follow_up: What do you mock, and what do you test with a real database?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: What was the hardest bug or technical challenge?
questions.answer: Describe the symptom, how you reproduced it, the evidence that identified the root cause, the fix, and how a regression test prevents recurrence.
questions.short_explanation: A specific truthful example is stronger than a generic claim.
questions.likely_follow_up: What did you try first that did not work?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: How would you deploy and configure the application?
questions.answer: Build a versioned artifact or container, externalize configuration, provide environment-specific secrets, run health checks, and use a repeatable CI/CD pipeline.
questions.short_explanation: The same artifact should be promoted across environments where possible.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you roll back a bad deployment?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: What metrics would you monitor?
questions.answer: Track request rate, latency percentiles, error rate, saturation, JVM heap/GC, thread pools, database pool usage and dependency failures.
questions.short_explanation: Metrics help detect symptoms; logs and traces help explain them.
questions.likely_follow_up: Which metric would alert you first for a slow API?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: How do you explain performance improvements credibly?
questions.answer: State the baseline, workload, measurement method, change and measured result; if no production measurements exist, describe the hypothesis and test instead.
questions.short_explanation: Do not invent percentages or traffic figures.
questions.likely_follow_up: How did you verify the change did not break correctness?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: What would you change if the project grew 10×?
questions.answer: Measure bottlenecks first; likely options include pagination, query/index tuning, caching, asynchronous work, connection-pool tuning and horizontal scaling.
questions.short_explanation: Do not introduce microservices or caching without a measured need.
questions.likely_follow_up: What is the first bottleneck you expect and why?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: How do you manage configuration and secrets?
questions.answer: Keep non-secret configuration external and inject secrets through a secure environment or secrets manager; restrict access and rotate credentials.
questions.short_explanation: Never commit passwords, private keys or production tokens.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you prevent secrets appearing in logs?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: How do you handle API version changes?
questions.answer: Prefer backward-compatible additions; introduce a new version or migration strategy for breaking contract changes and document deprecation timelines.
questions.short_explanation: Compatibility matters when multiple clients deploy independently.
questions.likely_follow_up: What if an old mobile app still calls the previous API?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: How do you review code from another developer?
questions.answer: Check correctness, readability, tests, security, query behavior, API compatibility and operational implications; ask questions respectfully and explain concerns with evidence.
questions.short_explanation: Code review should improve the design, not enforce personal style alone.
questions.likely_follow_up: What would block a pull request?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: How do you prioritize technical debt?
questions.answer: Assess risk, frequency of change, incident impact and cost of delay; schedule high-risk debt and avoid large rewrites without evidence.
questions.short_explanation: Technical debt is a trade-off that should be visible and managed.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you justify refactoring to a product manager?

questions.category: Project Deep Dive — Any Java Backend Project
questions.question: What would you do if you did not know an answer in an interview?
questions.answer: State what you know, make assumptions explicit, reason through alternatives and explain how you would verify the uncertain part.
questions.short_explanation: Honest structured reasoning is better than bluffing.
questions.likely_follow_up: What documentation or experiment would you consult?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Employee Management REST API
questions.question: What are the main resources and endpoints?
questions.answer: For example: GET /api/employees, GET /api/employees/{id}, POST /api/employees, PUT /api/employees/{id}, PATCH /api/employees/{id}, and DELETE /api/employees/{id}. Define status codes and DTOs for each.
questions.short_explanation: A resource-oriented contract is easier to document and test.
questions.likely_follow_up: Would DELETE be hard delete or soft delete?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Employee Management REST API
questions.question: What fields would you store for an employee?
questions.answer: A minimal model may include id, employeeCode, name, email, departmentId, status, createdAt and updatedAt. Add only fields required by the business and privacy policy.
questions.short_explanation: Use constraints for required and unique values.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you prevent duplicate employee codes?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Employee Management REST API
questions.question: How would you model departments?
questions.answer: Use a Department entity and a foreign-key relationship from Employee when employees belong to a department; enforce referential integrity in the database.
questions.short_explanation: The exact relationship depends on whether employees can belong to multiple departments.
questions.likely_follow_up: Would you use @ManyToOne, and what are its risks?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Employee Management REST API
questions.question: How would you implement search and pagination?
questions.answer: Accept validated page/size and allowlisted sort fields; use Pageable or a cursor strategy for large, frequently changing datasets.
questions.short_explanation: Never accept arbitrary SQL sort expressions from clients.
questions.likely_follow_up: What is the default maximum page size?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Employee Management REST API
questions.question: How do you handle an employee that does not exist?
questions.answer: Return 404 for a missing resource, using a domain-specific exception mapped by centralized exception handling.
questions.short_explanation: Avoid returning 200 with a confusing null body for a missing resource.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you distinguish missing from unauthorized?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Employee Management REST API
questions.question: How do you enforce unique email addresses under concurrent requests?
questions.answer: Add a database unique constraint and translate the resulting constraint violation into a suitable conflict response; an application pre-check alone is not enough.
questions.short_explanation: Two requests can pass a pre-check at the same time.
questions.likely_follow_up: Which HTTP status could represent a duplicate?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Employee Management REST API
questions.question: How would you implement soft deletion?
questions.answer: Add a status or deletedAt field and filter deleted records from normal queries; define how uniqueness, restoration and auditing work.
questions.short_explanation: Soft deletion affects every read path and retention policy.
questions.likely_follow_up: Can an email be reused after soft deletion?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Employee Management REST API
questions.question: How would you secure employee records?
questions.answer: Require authentication, role-based permissions, and object-level checks; restrict sensitive fields in DTOs and audit privileged operations.
questions.short_explanation: Hiding a button in the frontend is not authorization.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would HR and a normal employee permissions differ?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Employee Management REST API
questions.question: How would you audit changes?
questions.answer: Record actor, timestamp, action and relevant changed fields while minimizing sensitive data; use an audit table or a suitable auditing mechanism.
questions.short_explanation: Audit history should be protected from unauthorized modification.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you trace which user changed a salary field?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Employee Management REST API
questions.question: How would you test create/update operations?
questions.answer: Test valid requests, validation failures, duplicate constraints, missing IDs, unauthorized access and transaction rollback; use integration tests for persistence behavior.
questions.short_explanation: Tests should verify observable behavior, not only method calls.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you test pagination order?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: What entities are needed for a basic order service?
questions.answer: Common entities include Customer, Product, Inventory, Order, OrderItem, Payment and Shipment, with explicit ownership and status transitions.
questions.short_explanation: Separate business concepts instead of putting every field into one table.
questions.likely_follow_up: Which data must be consistent in one transaction?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: Walk through order creation.
questions.answer: Validate the cart and price, reserve inventory, create a pending order, initiate payment, then confirm or cancel based on payment outcome; define durable state transitions and failure recovery.
questions.short_explanation: Do not assume a payment provider and database share one transaction.
questions.likely_follow_up: What if payment succeeds but the callback is delayed?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: How do you prevent overselling inventory?
questions.answer: Use an atomic conditional update, row locking or another concurrency-safe reservation strategy, with a database constraint and clear reservation expiry.
questions.short_explanation: A read-then-write check without concurrency control can oversell.
questions.likely_follow_up: When would optimistic vs pessimistic locking fit?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: How do you handle duplicate order submissions?
questions.answer: Accept an idempotency key, persist it with the request outcome under a uniqueness constraint, and return the same outcome for safe retries.
questions.short_explanation: Network timeouts can leave clients unsure whether a request succeeded.
questions.likely_follow_up: What if the same key is reused with a different payload?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: Why should price be stored on OrderItem?
questions.answer: Store the agreed unit price and quantity at purchase time so historical orders remain correct when the current product price changes.
questions.short_explanation: An order is a financial record, not just a live view of the product catalog.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you handle discounts and tax calculations?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: How would you model order statuses?
questions.answer: Define allowed transitions such as PENDING_PAYMENT → CONFIRMED → SHIPPED → DELIVERED, with CANCELLED or REFUNDED paths and validation of transitions.
questions.short_explanation: An enum alone does not enforce valid transition rules.
questions.likely_follow_up: Can a delivered order become cancelled?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: What if payment succeeds but the order update fails?
questions.answer: Use a durable payment record, idempotent webhook processing, retries and reconciliation; for cross-service workflows, consider an outbox and saga-style compensation.
questions.short_explanation: External side effects cannot be rolled back by a local database transaction.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you reconcile stuck pending orders?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: How do you design payment webhook handling?
questions.answer: Verify the provider signature, persist the event or idempotency identifier, process it safely, and acknowledge only according to the provider's retry contract.
questions.short_explanation: Webhooks can be duplicated or arrive out of order.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you prevent a forged webhook?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: How would you process order confirmation emails?
questions.answer: Commit the order first, then publish a durable event or outbox record for an asynchronous worker to deliver the email with retries.
questions.short_explanation: Do not make a critical order transaction depend on a slow email server.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you avoid losing the event after database commit?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: How do you handle cancellations and refunds?
questions.answer: Validate the order state, release reserved inventory when appropriate, request the refund through an idempotent provider operation, and track refund status separately.
questions.short_explanation: Cancellation and refund are related but not always instantaneous.
questions.likely_follow_up: What if the refund provider is unavailable?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: How would you make order history efficient?
questions.answer: Index the customer and creation-time fields, paginate results, return summary DTOs, and load order-item details only when needed.
questions.short_explanation: Avoid fetching every order and relationship in one response.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you avoid the N+1 query problem?

questions.category: Project Case Study — E-commerce / Order Management
questions.question: What consistency is required for product search vs inventory?
questions.answer: Search results can often be eventually consistent, while inventory reservation and payment-related state require stronger transactional guarantees.
questions.short_explanation: Choose consistency based on business risk.
questions.likely_follow_up: Can the search page briefly show stale stock?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Local Farming Marketplace
questions.question: What is the core problem and first release scope?
questions.answer: Connect local growers with nearby buyers through product listings, seller contact details, availability and order/enquiry flows. Start with seller onboarding, listings, search by area, and contact/enquiry before building complex payments.
questions.short_explanation: A narrow MVP validates demand without unnecessary distributed-system complexity.
questions.likely_follow_up: Which feature would you deliberately postpone?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Local Farming Marketplace
questions.question: What domain entities would you design?
questions.answer: User, SellerProfile, ProductListing, ListingImage, Location, Enquiry or Order, and Notification; add Inventory or Payment only when the business workflow requires them.
questions.short_explanation: Separate the seller account from individual listings.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would one seller manage many listings?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Local Farming Marketplace
questions.question: How would you search listings by location?
questions.answer: For an MVP, filter by area or postal code and index those columns; if radius search is required, use database geospatial features or a dedicated search index when scale warrants it.
questions.short_explanation: Choose the simplest query that meets the product requirement.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you rank nearby listings?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Local Farming Marketplace
questions.question: How would you handle listing availability?
questions.answer: Store quantity or an availability status and update it through a concurrency-safe operation; define expiry and stale-listing cleanup rules.
questions.short_explanation: A listing page can be stale, so final availability must be checked at enquiry/order time.
questions.likely_follow_up: What happens if two buyers request the last item?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Local Farming Marketplace
questions.question: How would you verify sellers?
questions.answer: Use verified contact methods and a review/approval workflow appropriate to the marketplace; record verification status and restrict who can change it.
questions.short_explanation: Verification requirements depend on local law and the business model.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you handle a reported fraudulent seller?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Local Farming Marketplace
questions.question: How would you send SMS notifications?
questions.answer: Create a notification request after the relevant transaction, enqueue it durably, and use a worker with provider timeouts, retries, delivery status and rate limits.
questions.short_explanation: An SMS provider failure should not roll back a successful listing or order.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you avoid sending the same SMS twice?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Local Farming Marketplace
questions.question: How would you protect seller phone numbers?
questions.answer: Expose contact details only according to product policy, apply authorization and rate limits, minimize logs, and consider an in-app contact relay if privacy is important.
questions.short_explanation: Publicly exposing phone numbers can lead to scraping and spam.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you detect automated scraping?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Local Farming Marketplace
questions.question: How would you moderate listings?
questions.answer: Validate fields, restrict unsafe content, provide reporting, track moderation status and audit administrative actions.
questions.short_explanation: A review queue may be necessary as marketplace abuse grows.
questions.likely_follow_up: Would every listing need manual approval?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Local Farming Marketplace
questions.question: How would you design seller notifications for a new enquiry?
questions.answer: Persist the enquiry and a notification event atomically through an outbox or equivalent durable mechanism, then send asynchronously and retry safely.
questions.short_explanation: This avoids the database-commit/message-publish dual-write gap.
questions.likely_follow_up: What if the seller has opted out of SMS?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Local Farming Marketplace
questions.question: How would you prevent spam enquiries?
questions.answer: Use per-user and per-IP rate limits, verification where appropriate, duplicate detection and abuse monitoring, with privacy-aware retention.
questions.short_explanation: Rate limits should protect legitimate users too.
questions.likely_follow_up: What response should a rate-limited client receive?

questions.category: Project Case Study — Local Farming Marketplace
questions.question: How would you evolve the marketplace as traffic grows?
questions.answer: Measure first; add indexes and pagination, cache popular read-only listing data, move SMS to workers, use object storage/CDN for images, and split services only when organizational or scaling needs justify it.
questions.short_explanation: A modular monolith is often a good starting point.
questions.likely_follow_up: What would you keep in one database initially?

questions.question: What is the difference between functional and non-functional requirements?
questions.answer: Functional requirements describe system behavior; non-functional requirements describe qualities such as latency, availability, security, durability and cost.
questions.short_explanation: Clarify both before choosing components.
questions.likely_follow_up: Give three non-functional requirements for an order API.

questions.question: How do you clarify a system design question?
questions.answer: Ask who the users are, core use cases, scale, read/write mix, latency target, consistency needs, retention, security constraints and what is out of scope.
questions.short_explanation: This prevents overengineering the wrong problem.
questions.likely_follow_up: Which assumptions would you state aloud?

questions.question: How do you estimate capacity?
questions.answer: Estimate requests per second, average and peak traffic, data size, retention and bandwidth using explicit assumptions; add headroom and validate with load tests.
questions.short_explanation: Back-of-the-envelope math is for sizing direction, not false precision.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you estimate storage for one year of events?

questions.question: What is horizontal vs vertical scaling?
questions.answer: Vertical scaling increases resources on one machine; horizontal scaling adds instances and distributes work.
questions.short_explanation: Horizontal scaling usually requires stateless application instances and shared/durable state.
questions.likely_follow_up: What state makes an application hard to scale horizontally?

questions.question: What is a load balancer?
questions.answer: It distributes incoming traffic across healthy instances and can perform health checks and routing.
questions.short_explanation: It improves capacity and resilience but does not remove every bottleneck.
questions.likely_follow_up: What happens if every instance is unhealthy?

questions.question: What is stateless application design?
questions.answer: Each request carries or can retrieve the context it needs, rather than depending on in-memory state held by one instance.
questions.short_explanation: Sessions may be stored in a shared store or represented by signed tokens.
questions.likely_follow_up: What happens to an in-memory session during scale-out?

questions.question: What is caching and where can it be used?
questions.answer: Caching stores reusable results closer to the caller, such as in a browser, CDN, application cache or Redis.
questions.short_explanation: Define freshness, invalidation, capacity and behavior when the cache fails.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you avoid serving stale product prices?

questions.question: Explain cache-aside.
questions.answer: The application checks the cache, reads from the database on a miss, then populates the cache; updates typically invalidate or refresh the entry.
questions.short_explanation: It is simple but can experience stampedes or stale data.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you prevent many requests rebuilding the same missing key?

questions.question: What is a cache stampede?
questions.answer: Many requests miss the same key simultaneously and overload the backing store while recomputing it.
questions.short_explanation: Use request coalescing, locks, jittered expiry, stale-while-revalidate or prewarming where appropriate.
questions.likely_follow_up: What are the downsides of a distributed lock?

questions.question: What is database replication?
questions.answer: A primary or leader accepts writes and replicas copy changes for read scaling or resilience.
questions.short_explanation: Replication lag can make replica reads stale.
questions.likely_follow_up: Which reads should go to the primary?

questions.question: What is database sharding?
questions.answer: Sharding partitions data across multiple database nodes using a shard key.
questions.short_explanation: It can increase capacity but complicates joins, rebalancing and cross-shard transactions.
questions.likely_follow_up: What makes a poor shard key?

questions.question: SQL vs NoSQL: how do you choose?
questions.answer: Choose based on data relationships, transaction needs, query patterns, consistency, scaling and operational skills—not simply expected traffic.
questions.short_explanation: Relational databases can scale well; NoSQL is not automatically faster.
questions.likely_follow_up: Why might PostgreSQL be enough for an early-stage product?

questions.question: What is CAP theorem in practical terms?
questions.answer: During a network partition, a distributed system cannot guarantee both fully consistent responses and full availability for every request.
questions.short_explanation: The choice is made under partition conditions; real systems have nuanced guarantees.
questions.likely_follow_up: How might a shopping cart differ from a bank balance?

questions.question: Strong vs eventual consistency?
questions.answer: Strong consistency provides a current result according to the system's consistency model; eventual consistency permits temporary divergence that later converges.
questions.short_explanation: Use stronger guarantees for critical invariants and eventual consistency for suitable read models.
questions.likely_follow_up: Which marketplace data can tolerate a delay?

questions.question: What is a message queue used for?
questions.answer: It decouples producers and consumers, buffers bursts and supports asynchronous work such as notifications or report generation.
questions.short_explanation: Design for duplicate delivery, retries, poison messages and lag.
questions.likely_follow_up: What if the consumer is slower than the producer?

questions.question: What is at-least-once delivery?
questions.answer: A message is delivered one or more times, so consumers must safely handle duplicates.
questions.short_explanation: Idempotent processing is usually more practical than assuming exactly-once effects end to end.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you deduplicate an event?

questions.question: What is the transactional outbox pattern?
questions.answer: Write business data and an outbox event in the same database transaction; a separate publisher delivers the event and marks it processed.
questions.short_explanation: It avoids losing an event between database commit and message publication.
questions.likely_follow_up: Can the outbox publisher publish the same event twice?

questions.question: What is a saga?
questions.answer: A saga coordinates a distributed business transaction as local transactions with compensating actions for failures.
questions.short_explanation: It avoids requiring one global ACID transaction across services.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would an order saga compensate for a failed payment?

questions.question: What is a circuit breaker?
questions.answer: It temporarily blocks calls to a failing dependency and probes for recovery after a configured period.
questions.short_explanation: Combine it with timeouts, bounded retries and suitable fallbacks.
questions.likely_follow_up: Why can retries without a circuit breaker amplify an outage?

questions.question: What is backpressure?
questions.answer: It prevents a fast producer from overwhelming a slower consumer by limiting, buffering or slowing incoming work.
questions.short_explanation: Bound queues and define overload behavior rather than buffering indefinitely.
questions.likely_follow_up: What should the API do when capacity is exhausted?

questions.question: What is rate limiting?
questions.answer: It limits request volume per user, token, IP or resource over a time window.
questions.short_explanation: It protects capacity and reduces abuse; account for shared limits across instances.
questions.likely_follow_up: Compare fixed window, sliding window and token bucket.

questions.question: How do you make a service highly available?
questions.answer: Remove single points of failure, use health checks and redundant instances, replicate critical data, automate recovery and test failure scenarios.
questions.short_explanation: Availability depends on dependencies and operational practices, not just multiple servers.
questions.likely_follow_up: What if the database remains a single point of failure?

questions.question: What is graceful degradation?
questions.answer: The system preserves essential functions when a noncritical dependency is unavailable, for example by disabling recommendations while checkout continues.
questions.short_explanation: Fallbacks must not violate correctness or security.
questions.likely_follow_up: Which features can safely degrade in a marketplace?

questions.question: What is observability?
questions.answer: Logs, metrics and distributed traces provide complementary evidence about system behavior.
questions.short_explanation: Use correlation/trace IDs and avoid high-cardinality or sensitive labels.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you trace one request across three services?

questions.question: How do you plan for disaster recovery?
questions.answer: Define recovery time objective and recovery point objective, back up data, test restoration and document failover procedures.
questions.short_explanation: A backup that has never been restored is not a proven recovery plan.
questions.likely_follow_up: What is the difference between RTO and RPO?

questions.question: Design a URL shortener. What requirements do you clarify first?
questions.answer: Clarify create/redirect APIs, custom aliases, expiry, abuse prevention, analytics, expected read/write ratio, redirect latency and availability requirements.
questions.short_explanation: Redirect traffic is usually much higher than link creation.
questions.likely_follow_up: Do analytics need to be synchronous?

questions.question: What API endpoints would you define?
questions.answer: POST /api/urls creates a short link; GET /{code} redirects; optional authenticated endpoints retrieve or deactivate owned links.
questions.short_explanation: Keep redirect handling fast and define validation/error responses.
questions.likely_follow_up: Which endpoint needs authentication?

questions.question: How do you generate unique short codes?
questions.answer: Use a collision-resistant ID strategy such as a sequence/unique ID encoded in Base62, or random codes with a uniqueness constraint and collision retry.
questions.short_explanation: A database uniqueness constraint is the final correctness guard.
questions.likely_follow_up: What are the trade-offs of sequential IDs?

questions.question: How would you store and index short links?
questions.answer: Store code as a unique key with destination URL, owner, createdAt, expiry and status; index code for lookup and expiry for cleanup if needed.
questions.short_explanation: The redirect path should perform a narrow indexed lookup.
questions.likely_follow_up: Would you store click counts in the same hot row?

questions.question: How would you scale redirects?
questions.answer: Cache hot code-to-URL mappings, use stateless redirect instances, tune the database and consider read replicas or partitioning only when metrics justify them.
questions.short_explanation: Cache invalidation and expiry must be correct.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you invalidate a deleted or expired link?

questions.question: How would you count clicks without slowing redirects?
questions.answer: Return the redirect promptly and send click events asynchronously to a queue or stream, then aggregate them separately.
questions.short_explanation: Analytics can be eventually consistent if product requirements allow it.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you handle dropped analytics events?

questions.question: How do you prevent abuse?
questions.answer: Validate URL schemes, block dangerous destinations according to policy, rate-limit creation, detect spam/phishing, and provide reporting and takedown mechanisms.
questions.short_explanation: A shortener can become an abuse platform if unrestricted.
questions.likely_follow_up: Would you allow redirects to every URI scheme?

questions.question: Design a rate limiter for REST APIs.
questions.answer: Clarify whether limits are per user, API key, IP or endpoint, and define burst allowance, time window, distributed behavior and response headers.
questions.short_explanation: Different clients may need different policies.
questions.likely_follow_up: How should trusted internal services be treated?

questions.question: Compare fixed window, sliding window and token bucket.
questions.answer: Fixed window is simple but permits boundary bursts; sliding-window approaches smooth counting; token bucket allows controlled bursts at a configured refill rate.
questions.short_explanation: Select based on fairness, memory, precision and operational cost.
questions.likely_follow_up: Which would you choose for an API with bursty traffic?

questions.question: Where would you store distributed rate-limit state?
questions.answer: A shared store such as Redis can hold counters or token state; use atomic operations or scripts to avoid race conditions across instances.
questions.short_explanation: Per-process counters do not enforce a global limit.
questions.likely_follow_up: What happens when Redis is unavailable?

questions.question: Should a limiter fail open or fail closed?
questions.answer: Choose according to risk: fail closed protects expensive or sensitive operations; fail open may preserve availability for low-risk endpoints, with monitoring and fallback limits.
questions.short_explanation: There is no universal answer; make the security and availability trade-off explicit.
questions.likely_follow_up: What would you do for login attempts?

questions.question: How should a rate-limited request respond?
questions.answer: Return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests and, where useful, a Retry-After value or documented rate-limit headers.
questions.short_explanation: Clients should back off instead of retrying immediately.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you prevent retry storms?

questions.question: Design a notification service supporting email and SMS.
questions.answer: Provide an API to request a notification, persist the request or outbox event, enqueue work, route to provider adapters, retry transient failures and track delivery state.
questions.short_explanation: Separate business transactions from slow external providers.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you add push notifications later?

questions.question: What notification states would you track?
questions.answer: For example: ACCEPTED, QUEUED, SENDING, SENT_TO_PROVIDER, DELIVERED, FAILED and CANCELLED, with provider-specific states mapped carefully.
questions.short_explanation: Sent to provider does not necessarily mean delivered to the user.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you handle callbacks arriving out of order?

questions.question: How do you retry failed notifications?
questions.answer: Retry transient errors with exponential backoff and jitter, cap attempts, classify permanent failures, and move exhausted work to a dead-letter queue for review.
questions.short_explanation: Do not retry invalid phone numbers indefinitely.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you replay a dead-letter message safely?

questions.question: How do you avoid duplicate notifications?
questions.answer: Use a business event ID or idempotency key, persist deduplication state, and make provider calls as idempotent as the provider permits.
questions.short_explanation: End-to-end exactly-once delivery is generally difficult to guarantee.
questions.likely_follow_up: What if the provider accepts a message but your service times out?

questions.question: How do you manage provider outages?
questions.answer: Use timeouts, circuit breakers, bounded queues, retry policies and potentially a secondary provider for eligible messages.
questions.short_explanation: Switching providers may affect sender IDs, delivery guarantees and cost.
questions.likely_follow_up: When is fallback to a second provider unsafe?

questions.question: Design an order-management system at a high level.
questions.answer: Use an API layer, order service, relational store, inventory capability, payment-provider integration, durable event publishing, asynchronous notification workers and observability.
questions.short_explanation: Keep the initial architecture as simple as requirements allow.
questions.likely_follow_up: Which components need strong consistency?

questions.question: How do you reserve stock safely?
questions.answer: Use an atomic conditional decrement or a reservation record with concurrency control and expiry; confirm or release the reservation as the order progresses.
questions.short_explanation: A reservation avoids holding a database transaction open during a payment call.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do expired reservations get released?

questions.question: How do you coordinate order and payment state?
questions.answer: Represent payment and order as explicit state machines; process verified provider events idempotently and reconcile unresolved states.
questions.short_explanation: Do not assume callbacks arrive once or in order.
questions.likely_follow_up: What happens if a success event arrives after a timeout?

questions.question: How do you handle an event after the database commit?
questions.answer: Write an outbox row in the same transaction as the order update, then publish it asynchronously with retries.
questions.short_explanation: This removes the dual-write gap between database and broker.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do consumers handle duplicate events?

questions.question: What would you cache?
questions.answer: Potentially product descriptions, category data and read-heavy catalog responses; re-check price and inventory during the authoritative order operation.
questions.short_explanation: Never rely on a stale cache as the final stock reservation check.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you invalidate product data?

questions.question: How do you keep order history fast?
questions.answer: Use customer-and-time indexes, cursor or page-based pagination, summary projections and selective loading of line items.
questions.short_explanation: Avoid unbounded history responses and N+1 relationship loading.
questions.likely_follow_up: When would a read model or search index be useful?

questions.question: A database connection pool is exhausted. What do you inspect?
questions.answer: Check active/idle/pending connections, query latency, transaction duration, leaked connections, traffic and downstream waits; use timeouts and fix the cause before simply increasing pool size.
questions.short_explanation: A larger pool can overload the database and make latency worse.
questions.likely_follow_up: How can slow external calls inside transactions contribute?

questions.question: The JVM is using high CPU. How do you investigate?
questions.answer: Check process/container CPU, capture thread dumps or profiles, inspect hot methods, busy loops, lock contention and GC activity, then reproduce under a representative workload.
questions.short_explanation: A heap dump is mainly for memory analysis; CPU profiling and thread dumps often help first.
questions.likely_follow_up: What evidence points to GC overhead?

questions.question: Memory usage keeps increasing. What would you check?
questions.answer: Compare heap usage after GC, inspect heap dumps and dominator trees, look for retained collections, unbounded caches, listeners, thread locals and large buffers.
questions.short_explanation: High total process memory is not always a Java heap leak.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you distinguish a leak from normal cache growth?

questions.question: One API endpoint is slow only in production. Why?
questions.answer: Investigate data volume, query plans, indexes, network latency, traffic concurrency, configuration, JVM/container limits and downstream behavior.
questions.short_explanation: Production differs in cardinality and concurrency even when code is identical.
questions.likely_follow_up: How would you reproduce the issue safely?

questions.question: A deployment causes errors. What is your response?
questions.answer: Assess impact, stop further rollout or roll back using the deployment plan, preserve evidence, communicate status and verify recovery; then investigate root cause.
questions.short_explanation: Mitigation and learning are both important, but mitigation comes first.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you handle a database schema change during rollback?

questions.question: How do you make database migrations safer?
questions.answer: Use versioned migrations, backward-compatible expand-and-contract changes, backups where appropriate and validation on realistic data.
questions.short_explanation: Application versions may overlap during rolling deployments.
questions.likely_follow_up: Why add a nullable column before enforcing NOT NULL?

questions.question: What is a useful health check?
questions.answer: Liveness indicates whether the process should be restarted; readiness indicates whether it should receive traffic; dependency checks must avoid causing cascading failures.
questions.short_explanation: A slow dependency should not always cause every instance to restart.
questions.likely_follow_up: What is the risk of checking every dependency on liveness?

questions.question: How do you approach a production incident you have never seen?
questions.answer: Stabilize impact, gather evidence, identify a minimal hypothesis, test safely, communicate uncertainty and document follow-up actions.
questions.short_explanation: Avoid risky changes based on guesswork.
questions.likely_follow_up: What information belongs in a post-incident review?

questions.category: Java Implementation Choices in System Design
questions.question: How would you structure a Spring Boot codebase for a growing service?
questions.answer: Organize by feature/domain or by clear layers, keep controllers thin, define service-level use cases, isolate persistence and external clients, and keep shared utilities small.
questions.short_explanation: Package structure should reflect ownership and dependencies, not become a dumping ground.
questions.likely_follow_up: When is package-by-feature helpful?

questions.category: Java Implementation Choices in System Design
questions.question: How do you avoid blocking request threads on slow work?
questions.answer: Use asynchronous processing or a queue for noncritical work, configure bounded executors and timeouts, and return a suitable accepted response when processing is deferred.
questions.short_explanation: Asynchronous code adds failure handling and status tracking requirements.
questions.likely_follow_up: When should the API return 202 Accepted?

questions.category: Java Implementation Choices in System Design
questions.question: How do you choose a thread-pool size?
questions.answer: Measure CPU and blocking behavior, bound the queue, monitor saturation and tune under representative load; CPU-bound and I/O-bound workloads differ.
questions.short_explanation: There is no single correct pool size for every service.
questions.likely_follow_up: What happens with an unbounded executor queue?

questions.category: Java Implementation Choices in System Design
questions.question: When would you use virtual threads?
questions.answer: They can simplify high-concurrency blocking I/O workloads on supported Java versions, especially where thread-per-request code is natural.
questions.short_explanation: They do not eliminate database connection limits, CPU bottlenecks or the need for timeouts.
questions.likely_follow_up: What can still limit throughput with virtual threads?

questions.category: Java Implementation Choices in System Design
questions.question: How do you avoid N+1 queries in JPA?
questions.answer: Inspect generated SQL and query counts; use projections, fetch joins, entity graphs or batching where appropriate.
questions.short_explanation: Do not change every relationship to EAGER as a blanket fix.
questions.likely_follow_up: What problem can a large fetch join create?

questions.category: Java Implementation Choices in System Design
questions.question: What is optimistic locking?
questions.answer: Use a version field such as @Version to detect conflicting updates and reject or retry a stale write.
questions.short_explanation: It works well when conflicts are relatively uncommon.
questions.likely_follow_up: How should the API respond to a version conflict?

questions.category: Java Implementation Choices in System Design
questions.question: How do you prevent duplicate business operations at the database layer?
questions.answer: Use unique constraints, appropriate transactions and idempotency records; application checks alone are vulnerable to races.
questions.short_explanation: Database constraints are essential final guards for invariants.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you translate constraint violations into API errors?

questions.category: Java Implementation Choices in System Design
questions.question: How do you configure timeouts for outbound HTTP calls?
questions.answer: Set connection, response and overall operation timeouts according to the dependency and user-facing latency budget.
questions.short_explanation: Retries should fit within the total deadline.
questions.likely_follow_up: Why is a timeout required even if retries are configured?

questions.category: Java Implementation Choices in System Design
questions.question: How do you test concurrent updates?
questions.answer: Write integration tests that run competing operations and assert invariants, using the real transaction/isolation behavior where feasible.
questions.short_explanation: A sequential unit test will not expose every race condition.
questions.likely_follow_up: What invariant would you assert for stock quantity?

questions.category: Java Implementation Choices in System Design
questions.question: How do you prevent sensitive data from appearing in logs?
questions.answer: Use structured logging with allowlisted fields, redact secrets and personal data, review exception payloads, and test logging behavior.
questions.short_explanation: Request bodies and headers can contain credentials or private information.
questions.likely_follow_up: How do you correlate a request without logging its token?

recommended_practice_order: 1. Prepare a truthful 90-second project introduction and architecture diagram.
2. Practise the generic project deep-dive questions aloud.
3. Prepare one project deeply; know its schema, APIs, validation, transactions, security, tests and failure cases.
4. Practise system-design fundamentals before the case studies.
5. Draw URL shortener, rate limiter, notification service and order management designs without notes.
6. For each design, explain assumptions, bottlenecks, failure modes, trade-offs and what you would measure.
7. Review answers against your actual code so you can defend every technical claim.
